title: Fig. 1 .
summary: The introduction motivates teaching diverse algorithmic techniques using Sudoku puzzles as an accessible entry point, previewing three methods—simulated annealing, alternating projections, and backtracking—and noting that Sudoku is an NP-complete satisfiability problem where backtracking works for small instances but alternative strategies are needed for larger ones.

title: Backtracking.
summary: Backtracking is described as a depth-first search that orders empty cells by compatible-digit-list cardinality, grows partial solutions in dictionary order, and prunes infeasible subtrees en masse upon constraint violations; it is guaranteed to find all solutions when multiple exist.

title: Simulated Annealing.
summary: Simulated annealing is presented as a Markovian optimization method for Sudoku that defines cost as the number of constraint violations, proposes swaps between non-clue cells with probability proportional to their violation count, accepts uphill moves according to a temperature-dependent criterion, and cools the temperature geometrically toward zero.

title: Alternating Projections.
summary: Alternating projections is explained as a method that cycles through projections onto closed convex sets—in this case, simplex constraints representing row, column, and subgrid digit-frequency constraints on a continuous 3D probability tensor—and derives the O(d log d) Duchi et al. simplex projection algorithm used to solve the relaxed problem before imputing integer solutions.

title: Comparisons.
summary: Empirical comparisons show backtracking solved all 412 puzzles with the fastest run times, simulated annealing solved nearly all easy/medium puzzles but only 3% of the 95 hardest benchmarks, and alternating projection succeeded on 85% of easy and 41% of hard benchmark puzzles, sometimes outperforming backtracking on very hard cases.

title: Discussion.
summary: The discussion advocates teaching multiple combinatorial solution techniques using Sudoku as a culturally neutral pedagogical tool, highlights the contrast between exact methods that scale poorly and approximate methods that adapt better to large problems, and notes the potential relevance of alternating projections to harder combinatorial problems in fields like coding theory.
